lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Is this fair, Pluto? Me, dead at thirty, and Thoucritus, over ninety and still breathing?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Completely fair, Terpsion. He goes about his life without praying for any of his friends to die. You spent your entire life scheming against him, waiting for his estate.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: But shouldn't an old man who can't even enjoy his money anymore just step aside and make room for the young?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: You're legislating new laws, Terpsion: "Anyone who can no longer enjoy their money must die." Fate and Nature set a different schedule.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Then I blame the schedule! There ought to be a queue. The oldest goes first, then the next oldest. No cutting in line. You shouldn't have some super-geriatric still breathing—down to his last three teeth, practically blind, propped up by four servants, nose dripping, eyes crusty, totally oblivious to pleasure, a living tomb the young men laugh at—while gorgeous, strapping young men drop dead. It's rivers flowing backwards!

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Or at the very least, we should get an expiration date for each old man, so we don't waste time sucking up to the wrong ones. As it is, the proverb has it right: the cart is burying the ox.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Actually, Terpsion, the arrangement makes a lot more sense than you think. What possesses you people to gape at other people's property, throwing yourselves at childless old men to get adopted? You end up a total laughingstock when you get buried before them. Frankly, the public finds it highly entertaining. The more you pray for them to die, the sweeter it is for everyone when you beat them here.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: You've invented a whole new profession—falling madly in love with old men and women. Provided they're childless, of course; if they have kids, they're suddenly unlovable.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Though lately, a lot of your "beloveds" have figured out the scam. Even if they actually do have children, they pretend to hate them, just so they can attract a few "lovers" of their own. Then, when the will is read, the loyal hangers-on get shut out, the actual child and Nature win the day—as is only fair—and you legacy-hunters are left grinding your teeth.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: [sighs] You're right. I mean, look at how much Thoucritus bled me for! He always looked like he was about to drop. Whenever I walked in, he'd groan and croak deep in his chest like an unhatched chick.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: I thought he was one step away from the coffin, so I sent over piles of gifts so my rivals wouldn't outdo me in generosity. I lay awake most nights running the numbers, structuring the assets. That's what actually killed me, you know. Insomnia and stress. And him? After swallowing all my bait, he stood there at my funeral yesterday, laughing.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: [looking up, as if addressing the living world] Bravo, Thoucritus. Long may you live, getting richer and laughing at people like this. I hope you don't die until you've sent every single one of your flatterers to the grave.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: [pause] You know, Pluto, that actually makes me feel a lot better. I would love it if Charoiades died before Thoucritus too.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Don't worry, Terpsion. Pheidon, Melanthus—every last one of them is going to beat him down here, killed by the exact same stress.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: [laughs] I love it. Long live Thoucritus!
